questions.prompt: What does price do in Chapter 10 besides signal cost?
choices: It can act as an expectation cue that changes perceived effectiveness.
It always guarantees higher quality.
It removes all uncertainty from a purchase.

explanation.gentle: The chapter argues that price can shape how effective something feels.
explanation.direct: Price behaves here like a placebo signal, not just a cost number.
explanation.competitive: The tag can start acting like part of the dose.

questions.prompt: Why can an identical product feel stronger at a higher price?
choices: Because the higher price loads expectation of potency into the experience.
Because expensive items always contain different ingredients.
Because buyers stop noticing results.

explanation.gentle: Expectation carried by price can change the felt result.
explanation.direct: The premium cue alters perceived efficacy even when substance stays the same.
explanation.competitive: The number helps manufacture the effect.

questions.prompt: How is this chapter different from a simple anchoring chapter?
choices: It is about felt effectiveness, not only reference points for spending.
It rejects all pricing psychology.
It focuses only on discounts.

explanation.gentle: Ariely is showing that price can change experience, not just willingness to pay.
explanation.direct: This mechanism goes from cost cue to efficacy cue.
explanation.competitive: The tag gets into the effect, not just the bid.

questions.prompt: Why is the chapter ethically tense?
choices: Because the same mechanism can create relief in one setting and manipulation in another.
Because price is always immoral.
Because medicine and markets never overlap.

explanation.gentle: A price-driven expectation can help or mislead depending on the context.
explanation.direct: The same placebo-style cue can comfort in medicine and distort in consumer sales.
explanation.competitive: One cue can heal a little or hustle a lot.

questions.prompt: What practical move best fits Ariely's advice here?
choices: Test what survives after the premium price cue is weakened or hidden.
Assume the most expensive option is always best.
Ignore all evidence except reputation.

explanation.gentle: Cleaner comparisons help reveal what the item itself contributes.
explanation.direct: You want to separate actual efficacy from the power of the price signal.
explanation.competitive: Take the premium theater out and rerun the result.

questions.prompt: What does the chapter suggest about medical and consumer settings?
choices: They share the mechanism even when the ethical feeling is different.
They never influence each other.
They cancel the effect out.

explanation.gentle: The same expectation carried by price appears in both domains.
explanation.direct: Ariely keeps both settings visible because the psychology overlaps.
explanation.competitive: The clinic and the store can be running the same trick with different vibes.

questions.prompt: What is Ariely not saying in this chapter?
choices: That every expensive product is fraudulent and price never carries information.
That price can distort felt efficacy.
That expectation matters.

explanation.gentle: The chapter allows that some prices reflect real differences.
explanation.direct: Ariely's warning begins when the cue outruns the evidence, not whenever price is high.
explanation.competitive: The problem is cost pretending to be proof, not cost existing.

questions.prompt: What happens when price outruns evidence?
choices: The price cue can start doing more of the healing or persuading than the thing itself.
The item automatically becomes worthless.
People stop caring about price altogether.

explanation.gentle: That is when price becomes a stronger part of the experience than it should.
explanation.direct: The signal starts manufacturing efficacy instead of merely describing value.
explanation.competitive: The tag starts playing the lead role.

questions.prompt: Why do hidden-price tests matter in this chapter?
choices: They reduce the chance that price acts like a placebo cue in the evaluation.
They guarantee perfect neutrality forever.
They make quality impossible to judge.

explanation.gentle: Removing the cue helps reveal what the thing itself contributes.
explanation.direct: A lower-frame comparison reduces contamination from priced expectation.
explanation.competitive: It gives the product a chance to win without its expensive costume.

questions.prompt: How does Chapter 10 prepare the move into The Context of Our Character, Part 1?
choices: It keeps showing that context cues can shape outcomes more than stable trait stories admit.
It proves character never matters.
It ends the book's concern with context.

explanation.gentle: The chapter keeps building the larger idea that setups shape behavior and experience.
explanation.direct: It prepares the honesty chapters by extending the role of situational cues.
explanation.competitive: If a price tag can bend the effect, context can probably bend conscience too.
